topic: Openbot (CopilotKit): AI Coworkers That Each Get Their Own Browser
summary: OpenBot is CopilotKit's MIT-licensed, self-hosted platform for 'AI coworkers' in which every agent gets its own computer — a container with its own Chromium, its own browser profile holding real logins, its own /workspace volume and its own shell. Its distinguishing claim is ordering, not features: every browser click, file read, shell command and MCP call loops back through a single server-side gateway that resolves the target, evaluates a CEL policy, writes an audit row and only then acts. CopilotKit authors the AG-UI protocol, so any AG-UI endpoint (LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK, Microsoft Agent Framework, or hand-written) becomes a governed coworker without being rewritten. The honest verdict for a 2026 reader is a split one. On architecture, OpenBot is the most complete open-source answer to the trust gap that Deloitte and McKinsey both identify as the #1 brake on agentic AI scaling (only 21% of enterprises have mature agentic-AI governance; nearly two-thirds name security and risk the top barrier to scaling). On maturity, it is six weeks old, alpha, ships breaking changes every few days (451 commits, ~33 contributors, v0.0.15 as of 2026-09-22) and — critically — its shipped default policy is deny: [] / allow: ["true"], meaning 'fails closed' describes what the engine does when a rule breaks, not what the box does on day one. It is genuinely self-hosted except for one dependency that is not optional: durable threads and memory require CopilotKit Intelligence (free tier, self-hostable), and the API server refuses to start without an Intelligence project and license token. The category it competes in is now crowded — SpaceXAI's Grok Bot ($120/seat/mo teams, $200/mo individual), Anthropic's Claude Cowork (now folded into Claude, with a built-in browser), and OpenAI's Dots (GPT-6 Astra, own cloud computer, 4,000+ apps, announced 2026-09-29) — but OpenBot is the only one of those you can fork, inspect and run on your own hardware.

product_facts.gateway_sequence: resolve the target from a server-held page snapshot (a Bot cannot invent an element reference) -> evaluate the current action policy -> write an audit row for the decision -> only then call the Bot's computer -> write a second row if the forwarded action fails. No path acts without the record existing first.
product_facts.policy_engine: CEL (Common Expression Language). Inspectable fields include tool.name, intent, bot.id, actor.id, page.url, page.host, element.*, key, command, file.*, mcp.* and initiator.* (so a rule can refuse a scheduled routine what it would allow a person). Deny is evaluated before allow; a missing policy permits nothing; a broken rule refuses rather than opens.
product_facts.day_one_policy_caveat: Verified against the repo, and it corrects a claim several secondary sources get wrong. With AGENT_COMPUTER_POLICY unset, .env.example states the built-in default 'permits the acting tools and forbids nothing, and records every action either way' — so the out-of-box posture is permissive but fully audited. What fails closed is the engine, not the box: 'deny is evaluated first and beats allow. An empty allow permits nothing, a missing policy permits nothing, and a rule that fails to parse denies rather than letting the action through. The server refuses to start if this is set and malformed, so an invalid restriction never falls back to permissive behavior.' One source (ssdnodes) states flatly that 'policy is deny-by-default', which its own primary sources do not support — worth noting as the kind of error that propagates. The safe adoption path is built in: mode 'dry-run' decides and records but lets everything through, and v0.0.5 added a UI dry-run against past activity, so a new rule can be tested before it refuses anybody's work. mode 'enforce' is what actually blocks.
product_facts.isolation: COMPUTER_SUPERVISOR_URL unset means Bots share one computer (a meaningfully weaker guarantee). Computers bind to loopback only and every request must present a token scoped to that specific container. COMPUTER_RUNTIME=runsc switches containers to gVisor where the host supports it. SPIRE workload-identity services are defined in the compose file but the shipped start script leaves them off.
product_facts.hardening: Browser navigation is limited to plain http/https; anything resembling a cloud metadata address is refused regardless of configuration; the same validation applies to custom agent endpoints; auth headers for those endpoints are stored write-only. PostgreSQL sits on a separate Docker network reachable only by the server and migrations, so a Bot talked into running psql finds nothing to connect to. A shell command inherits PATH, locale, terminal and proxy variables but not the rest of the deployment environment, so KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not in its env.
product_facts.egress_identity: Per-Bot egress identity via EGRESS_PROXY_<BOT> / EGRESS_PROXY_DEFAULT, so the far side sees a stable address it can allow-list or attribute to a specific Bot. Proxy credentials may sit in the URL and are split out before Playwright sees them; only the HOST is ever reported back on the admin page or API, so the password never lands on a screen. The docs are explicit that this is attribution, not anonymity, and not a boundary by itself. These belong in egress.env beside .env, not in .env — in .env they reach no process and the browser goes out directly with nothing saying so, a silent failure mode worth flagging.
product_facts.human_handoff: At a login wall or 2FA prompt the Bot stops and flags a person rather than guessing a way around it. Control moves into the same live-view panel and each stage is logged as computer.help_requested, computer.control_taken, computer.control_released. While a person is driving, Bot actions are refused rather than queued.
product_facts.secrets: Credentials are stored through /admin/credentials, encrypted at rest, never returned by an API, and the transcript records that a secret was requested and how long it was — never what it said.
product_facts.shipped_coworkers: Thirteen coworkers in the example tenant package (examples/fintech/), defined as YAML configuration rather than code: General Assistant, Knowledge, a Risk Analyst reached as an endpoint, and ten single-job agents (expense claim vs policy, meeting note to follow-ups, release notes, ticket triage, new-starter handbook Q&A, briefs that name what could not be found, interview write-ups, on-call handover, renewal prep, customer-feedback theming).
product_facts.skills_model: Skills are instructions, not capabilities. The tool set offered on a run is the intersection of the skill's declared tool list and the Bot's grants. A Bot holding more than twelve tools is offered, per run, only the tools of the skills that match the incoming message — which is what makes 'smarter tool use' work and is also why a deployment with no skills never narrows.
required_env: MANAGED_AGENT_AG_UI_URL + MANAGED_AGENT_TOKEN (or the managed Bot is omitted)
product_facts.setup_effort: Docker + Bun 1.3+. .env.example has ten blank keys of which only three are yours to fill; scripts/start.sh generates the rest. .env.example ships OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true, which admits every request as one administrator, so a fresh clone reaches the product without registering an OAuth client — sign-in must be turned on before anyone else can reach the deployment. A prompt.txt in the repo root is written to be pasted into an AI assistant to do the whole setup.
product_facts.enterprise_features: SSO via Google/Microsoft/Okta from the environment, plus company SAML or OIDC providers registered at runtime and routed by email domain. Helm chart for Kubernetes proven on a real AWS cluster; each Bot gets its own isolated computer that suspends when idle while keeping its logins. Scheduled routines run with their creator's permissions and switch themselves off with a notice if they keep failing. Bot-to-bot delegation is opt-in per pair.
product_facts.connectors: Google Drive (read-only) and Notion (read-write) ship first-party; each person connects their own account so a Bot only ever sees what that person may see, and answers link the live file rather than a stored copy. v0.0.12 (2026-09-15) added Composio (COMPOSIO_API_KEY) brokering a few hundred SaaS apps behind one account. Custom MCP servers must pass URL checks; unknown tools and custom-server tools are treated as writes.

key_points: The most thorough independent English review; states 5,107 stars / 649 forks / 17 open issues as of 2026-09-18 and v0.0.12 as current.

Frames the enterprise blocker precisely: 'a security team cannot say where the browser session went, what the agent clicked, or which rule would have stopped it' — and notes OpenBot is built audit-trail-first and chat-UI-second, which is what separates it from the dozens of browser-agent repos.
Best explanation of the hub-with-one-door architecture and of why a Bot framework is irrelevant to governance: 'a LangGraph agent gets the same gate as a 40-line hand-written AG-UI endpoint.'
Flags the detail worth copying even without adopting OpenBot: skills are instructions, not capabilities — listing find-a-document loads nothing until an admin connects Drive and grants those tools.
Names the real costs up front: a month old, a template you fork, and it needs CopilotKit Intelligence running somewhere.

Proposes a concrete one-hour evaluation: clone, pin the release, write three deny rules in /admin/boundaries, ask the General Assistant to fill out httpbin.org/forms/post, then open /admin/audit and ask whether a compliance lead would sign off on that page.

The most technically sceptical review, and the source of the single most important caveat: 'the shipped default is deny: [] and allow ["true"], which permits everything until an administrator writes a restrictive rule. "Fails closed" describes what happens when the policy breaks, not what the box does on day one.'
Documents the weaker-by-default isolation mode: with COMPUTER_SUPERVISOR_URL unset, Bots share one computer — a meaningfully weaker guarantee than the headline 'a computer each'.
Notes COMPUTER_RUNTIME=runsc switches to gVisor and that SPIRE workload-identity services are defined in the compose file but left off by the shipped start script.
Confirms the cloud-metadata refusal applies to custom agent endpoints too, not just page navigation, and that endpoint auth headers are stored write-only.
Supplies the company context: OpenBot's first alpha was 2026-08-17, three more tags inside five days, and CopilotKit raised $27M led by Glilot Capital, NFX and SignalFire in May 2026.
Enumerates the eight moving parts and their ports, matching docs/architecture.md.
The most useful non-vendor account for a security/compliance reader, written as a tool check rather than a review.

States the case for why per-agent isolation matters: 'Agents become risky when they move beyond answering questions and can operate signed-in websites, files, and commands. A confirmation dialog alone is often insufficient.'
Draws the boundary that marketing blurs: 'Policy controls actions but does not automatically validate business correctness. An allowed click can still be wrong.'
Warns that a Bot with browser, shell and MCP access has a large attack surface, and that prompt injection, malicious files and compromised tools remain real risks.

Its recommended first test is the strongest practical advice found: a narrowly scoped read-only workflow on test accounts, deny-by-default policy, five known tasks, and a manual comparison of the audit trail against the resulting output.
Its 40-supplier-portal walkthrough (download only PDFs, block payments/profile changes/shell, human at the 2FA prompt) is the concrete workflow pattern a review post should reproduce.

Vendor primary source for the feature set most reviews cite: first-party Google Drive and Notion connectors, bot-to-bot delegation, scheduled routines, smart message routing, take-the-wheel-on-demand, skill-scoped tool narrowing, enterprise SSO, and a Helm chart.
Documents the Kubernetes story concretely: Helm chart proven on a real AWS cluster, each Bot's computer suspends when idle to keep costs down, works on EKS/GKE/AKS or your own cluster.
Announces the rule dry-run: admins can test a boundary rule against past activity to see what it would have blocked — the mitigation for the deny-by-default caveat.

Routine semantics matter for governance: a routine runs with its creator's permissions, 'it can do exactly what they could do in chat, nothing more,' and switches itself off with a notice if it keeps failing.
Confirms star milestones chronologically (3,500 at v0.0.5 on 2026-09-01), useful for the growth curve.
Covers the founders' 2026-09-22 four-agent travel demo pitting OpenBot against Grok Bot — and, unusually for this category, refuses to treat it as evidence.

The methodological critique is the best available and should be reused: the posts published no prompt, models, tool permissions, browser state, starting context, completion times, costs, raw traces or scoring rubric, and identified no measured winner — 'matching agent names and an initial prompt controls only a small part of an agent run.'

States the actual product thesis cleanly: Grok Bot supplies models, cloud computers and interface as a hosted service; OpenBot gives organizations source code and infrastructure controls and leaves deployment, model selection and operation to them.
Confirms Grok Bot's timeline: launched 2026-08-11, expanded across SuperGrok and Cursor subscriptions, opened to enterprise on 2026-09-03 with access, network and audit controls.
Repeats the vendor-reported 3,500-star milestone and v0.0.14 (2026-09-21) as current at time of writing.
Best FAQ-shaped framing and the clearest statement of the non-obvious dependency: 'the repo is MIT. The quick start is not clone and go.'

Lists the env vars the API server refuses to start without, and notes durable threads and memory live in CopilotKit Intelligence, not local Postgres — conversations survive restarts because Intelligence stores them.
Corrects the common misreading of the pitch: OpenBot is not a Grok Bot clone, it is the same shape (persistent computer + real logins) with you hosting it.
States the launch reach numbers: the announcement post crossed 438.5K views in a day; the repo hit 1.1k stars and 105 forks within about a week.
Flags the honest state of the project: alpha, default no-auth (OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true), and open issues about authorization and policy holes — not production-ready.

The benchmark context a review should use instead of repeating vendor claims: Browser Use 89.1% on WebVoyager, OpenAI's Computer-Using Agent 87% on the same benchmark, Claude Opus 4.7 at 82.3% on OSWorld.

Makes the key 2026 point about benchmarks: WebVoyager is saturated — several agents now report above 90%, and once a benchmark clusters that tightly it can no longer discriminate. A high score means competent, not best.

Explains the architectural fork OpenBot bets against: DOM-reading agents (Browser Use) are fast and token-efficient on clean markup but browser-only by construction; pixel-reading agents (Computer Use, CUA) are slower and token-heavy but can drive a canvas app, a PDF viewer or a legacy desktop tool.
Notes Operator no longer exists standalone — OpenAI folded it into ChatGPT Agent in 2025 — which matters when a comparison table lists it as a live product.
Its 'the sandbox matters as much as the agent itself' argument is the bridge from this comparison into OpenBot's per-Bot container thesis.

angles: Ordering is the product. OpenBot's differentiator is not isolation or policy as a feature list but the fixed sequence — resolve, evaluate, write the audit row, then act — so no action can complete before its own record exists. That inverts the usual 'agent acts, then we log it' posture and is the single most useful thing to explain to a reader comparing it to a chat agent with a pile of MCP servers.

Verify 'fails closed' before you trust it. The engine fails closed — a missing policy permits nothing and a broken rule denies — but the out-of-box posture is permissive: with AGENT_COMPUTER_POLICY unset the built-in default permits the acting tools and forbids nothing, while recording every action either way. Treat deny-by-default as configuration you must perform, not a property you inherit, and use mode 'dry-run' (or the v0.0.5 UI dry-run against past activity) to test a rule before it starts refusing real work. Note too that at least one widely-read source states flatly that 'policy is deny-by-default', which the primary docs do not support — a good illustration of how this caveat gets lost in retelling.

Self-hosting is now the answer to a measured trust gap, not a philosophical preference. McKinsey finds nearly two-thirds name security and risk the top barrier to scaling agentic AI and only about a third reach maturity level 3+ on agentic governance; Deloitte finds only 21 percent have mature agentic-AI governance, i.e. ~80 percent lack decision boundaries, monitoring and audit trails. That is the number that justifies this product category existing.

The boundary is drawn per agent, not per person — and that is the load-bearing security claim. A login one Bot holds is not one the next Bot can pick up, because each has its own container, browser profile and /workspace. Note honestly that COMPUTER_SUPERVISOR_URL unset collapses this to one shared computer, so the guarantee is configuration-dependent.

Governance rides the protocol, not the framework. Because CopilotKit authors AG-UI, a LangGraph, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or hand-written endpoint gets the identical gate. For a reader who already has an agent, this is the difference between adopting OpenBot and rewriting for it.

Sandbox escapes are a live 2026 research topic. AISI's SandboxEscapeBench and CSA's 'Week of Sandbox Escapes' mean the container boundary is exactly where the interesting failures are. gVisor (COMPUTER_RUNTIME=runsc) is opt-in and SPIRE workload identity ships switched off — say so rather than implying the strongest mode is the default.

Total cost is the least transparent part. The software is MIT and there is no per-seat price, but a running deployment needs Docker, Bun 1.3+, PostgreSQL with pgvector, a CopilotKit Intelligence project and license token that the server refuses to start without, plus your own model keys, plus operator time. Set that against Grok Bot's $120/seat/month ($200 individual) and be explicit that the trade is money for control and responsibility.

Alpha risk is quantified, not vague: 451 commits and ~33 contributors in six weeks, v0.0.15, breaking changes every few days, and open issues asking for a pluggable policy evaluation point (the rules are injectable, the evaluator is not) and reporting that a coworker created as 'Built in' still cannot hand work on. Pin a release and expect to read release notes.

The benchmark honesty angle: every vendor in this category ships a demo, and the founders' own Grok Bot travel comparison published no prompt, models, permissions, costs, traces or rubric. Reuse the methodological critique — it is the strongest reason a reader should trust an architecture teardown over a side-by-side video.

The evaluation is cheap and decisive, and saying so is more useful than a score. Clone it, pin a release, write three deny rules in /admin/boundaries, run one narrowly scoped read-only task on a test account, then open /admin/audit and ask whether a compliance lead would sign off on that page. That takes about an hour and tests the only claim that matters.

faq.q: Is OpenBot the same as Grok Bot?
faq.a: No. Same shape — a persistent agent with its own computer and real logins — but OpenBot is self-hosted, MIT-licensed source you fork and operate, while Grok Bot is a hosted service from SpaceXAI at $120/seat/month for teams and $200/month for individuals. You do not get Grok Bot's VM image, policy engine or audit log as a repo.

The code is MIT. A running deployment is not. It needs Docker, Bun 1.3+, PostgreSQL with pgvector, your own model keys, and a CopilotKit Intelligence project plus COPILOTKIT_LICENSE_TOKEN that the API server refuses to start without. Intelligence holds durable threads and memory (local Postgres holds product data, policy, audit, credentials, grants and channels). A free Intelligence plan exists and Intelligence can be self-hosted.

Any endpoint that speaks AG-UI: LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK, the Claude Agent SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework, or a hand-written endpoint. Governance lives in the gateway, so the framework choice does not change what is enforced.

No. It is explicitly alpha and described by its own README as a template to clone rather than a product, with breaking changes landing every few days. Ship it behind a pilot, pin a release, and run a narrowly scoped test first.

faq.q: Does it fail closed by default?
faq.a: Not out of the box. The engine refuses on a missing or broken policy, but the shipped default is deny: [] with allow: ["true"], which permits everything until an administrator writes a restrictive rule at /admin/boundaries. Treat deny-by-default as configuration you must perform, and use the rule dry-run added in v0.0.5 to test rules against past activity first.
Yes. v0.0.5 shipped a Helm chart proven on a real AWS cluster, with each Bot's computer isolating itself and suspending when idle while keeping its logins. EKS, GKE, AKS or your own cluster.

faq.q: What happens when a Bot hits a login or 2FA prompt?
faq.a: It stops and asks a person instead of guessing a way around it. Control transfers into the same live-view panel and each stage is logged (computer.help_requested, computer.control_taken, computer.control_released). While a human is driving, Bot actions are refused rather than queued.

Credentials are stored through /admin/credentials, encrypted at rest, never returned by an API, and never injected into the model context — the audit trail records that a secret was requested and how long it was, not what it said.
